title: Illuminating Notch receptor-ligand selectivity through structure-guided protein engineering supplement
text:
Notch signaling guides cell fate decisions and influences the pathogenesis of inherited and acquired human
diseases. In this R35 proposal, we will integrate synthetic, structural, and cellular biology to determine how
emerging classes of extracellular regulatory proteins mediate crosstalk between Notch and other major
developmental pathways. Additionally, we will engineer protein biologics that can modulate the activity of
mechanosensitive Notch proteins for applications in regenerative medicine.

title: Oncogenic triggers and their influence on 3D chromosomal architecture
text:
PROJECT 3: PROJECT NARRATIVE
In this project we focus on T cell acute leukemia-specific 3D “cis regulatory element (CRE) hubs”, DNA elements
that interact with multiple other DNA areas, including promoters and enhancers. We hypothesize that CRE hubs
coordinate cell type specific gene networks serving as 'headquarters' of cell identity and are able to control
transformation, tumor progression and response to drug treatment.

title: Leveraging the biphasic life cycle of a non-vertebrate chordate to investigate developmental transitions and phenotypic plasticity
text:
Human development and survival depends greatly on how and when individual cells decide to
proliferate, lay dormant, or carry out specialized functions like the formation of muscle fibers
through cell-cell fusion. We will use the small, transparent embryos of Ciona, one of the
invertebrates most closely related to humans, to better understand which genes are activated to
allow certain cells to survive the remarkable remodeling of the animal during metamorphosis from
the larval to the adult phase. We will also study the process of cell-cell fusion in Ciona, which is
shared with humans and other vertebrates.

title: Refining iPSC-Based Spinal Cord Model Systems by Fabricating Developmentally Programmed Extracellular Matrix Cues
text:
The purpose of our proposed study is to refine induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC)-neuronal model systems by
providing developmentally appropriate extracellular matrix (ECM) cues. We will first define the composition and
nature of remodeling of the mammalian CNS matrisome in vivo, and then leverage our combined expertise in
iPSC technologies and biomaterials to establish ECM mimetic matrices that can recapitulate the architecture
and modulatory activity of the physiological matrisome and facilitate the maturation and aging of stem cell derived
neuronal models in vitro.

title: Passive digital phenotyping for capturing real-world neurobehavior in neurodegenerative disease
text:
Innovative methods to improve timely and accurate detection of Alzheimer's disease and related dementias are
urgently needed for optimizing dementia care. We propose to leverage passively collected smartphone data
capturing smartphone interactions (via screen use and battery data) and everyday activity (via accelerometer
and GPS data), and evaluate their utility to detect neurobehavioral impairment in frontotemporal dementia and
Alzheimer's disease. We will further validate their clinical relevance by testing baseline and longitudinal
associations with gold-standard in-person cognitive tests and biomarkers of neurodegeneration.

title: ECOG-ACRIN Network Group Operations Center
text:
The primary goal of ECOG-ACRIN is to provide the support necessary to conduct relevant and
rigorous clinical trials, which benefit public health by improving survival and the quality of life
and standard of care for cancer patients.

title: MG53 function in muscle aging
text:
Elderly individuals are susceptible to injury and have reduced capacity to repair injured muscle, ultimately leading
to muscle weakness and loss of physical activity. By using biochemistry, cell and molecular biology, genome
editing, and in vivo animal models, our proposed studies shall provide critical insights into the biology underlying
diminished myokine function of MG53 in muscle aging and the potential of rejuvenating muscle satellite cells
with inducible secretion of MG53 to enhance muscle repair and regeneration for treating aging-related muscle
dysfunction.

title: The role of tyrosine metabolism in tuberculosis pathogenesis
text:
Tuberculosis (TB) remains a leading cause of death from infectious diseases globally. Understanding why some
infected individuals develop disease and others do not is paramount to developing preventative treatments. We
discovered an unexpected association between TB susceptibility and inhibition of tyrosine metabolism, which
could be leveraged as a novel target for preventative therapy against TB progression.

title: Reducing Lung Cancer Risk among Appalachian Women Using Community‐Engaged Intervention Research
text: Lung cancer is the leading cause of cancer-related death among women, including high rates in the Appalachian region. The objectives of this R00 proposal will support the reduction of lung cancer incidence and mortality among Appalachian women by developing, adapting, and pilot testing an evidence-based intervention in collaboration with community partners. This study will inform the future submission of an R01 to test the efficacy of the developed intervention.

title: A computer-vision guided automated microinjection system with increased robustness, throughput, and generalizability to diverse species
text:
Objective Biotechnology has developed an instrument, the Autoinjector, that automates the labor and skill-
intensive process of microinjection into embryos for transgenesis, gene editing, and other applications. This
project aims to build on a successful SBIR Phase I grant that has put us on a path to implement a robust,
production-scale commercial Autoinjector with increased throughput and generalizability for human out-of-the-
loop microinjection and broad applicability to diverse species. Our automated microinjection system will make
these techniques more accessible, reduce costs, and dramatically increase the scale at which such
experiments can be carried out, broadly accelerating discovery related to human health and disease in animal
research models, and thus this proposal is relevant to most NIH Institutes.
We will implement multi-pipette capabilities to mitigate needle clogging and to enable multiplexed experiments
and will robustly test these improvements over the course of more than 500 injection experiments in
partnership with Drosophila researchers at Baylor College of Medicine. Finally, to expand beyond our
beachhead market, we will develop software tools that enable users to train new computer vision models to
apply the Autoinjector to a wide range of additional species.

title: Mass Spectrometry Molecular Imaging and Multi-Omics
text: The Sidney Kimmel Comprehensive Cancer Center (SKCCC) Mass Spectrometry Molecular Imaging and Multi-Omics (MSMIMO) Shared Resource (SR) integrates three cooperative facilities across Johns Hopkins: the Applied Imaging Mass Spectrometry (AIMS) facility, the Mass Spectrometry and Proteomics (MSP) facility, and the Metabolomics unit. The MSMIMO SR offers innovative, integrated multiomic workflows that combine omic technologies for systems biology analysis of cancer cells and tissues using state-of-the-art and novel mass spectrometry-based technologies for molecular tissue imaging (spatialomic), metabolomic and proteomic strategies to accelerate cancer research. AIMS offers rapid matrix-assisted laser desorption/ionization (MALDI) imaging of a variety of biomolecules, including endogenous peptides, proteins, N-glycans, lipids, metabolites, and drugs or drug metabolites in cancer cells, spheroids, organoids or tissue sections at high spatial resolution (5 micron). The MSP Facility offers proteomic labeling and label-free strategies, including multidimensional protein identification technology, parallel reaction monitoring, tandem mass tags and stable isotopic labeled amino acids in cell culture for identification and relative or targeted quantification of novel therapeutic proteins, modifications or pathways, dysregulated in cancers, and for tracking interactions of these targets during changes in signal transduction or formation of protein complexes. The Metabolomics Unit offers high throughput detection and quantification of polar and nonpolar metabolites in tissue or fluid extracts. MSMIMO SR services include experimental design, tissue sectioning, sample preparation, buffer exchange, proteolysis, labeling, derivatizations, chromatography, MALDI imaging, tandem mass spectrometry imaging, image analysis, two-dimensional nanoflow liquid chromatography tandem mass analysis, data analysis and interpretation, and assistance with reporting results, training and data submission to public repositories. Biostatisticians and Bioinformaticians are available for in-depth statistical analyses of spatialomic, metabolomic and proteomic results. The MSMIMO SR provides access and training to proprietary software and equipment for SKCCC investigators who wish to perform their own analysis and offers workshops on operating user- accessible mass spectrometers several times a year. The MSMIMO SR's innovative approaches and workflows provide SKCCC Members with the spatial resolution to compare metabolomes, drug metabolism, lipidomes and proteomes across individual cells or cell clusters within the tumor microenvironment. Our comprehensive, highly multiplexed molecular discovery platforms are designed to advance Center Members' research by revealing molecular networks that drive tumorigenesis. During this funding period, 63 SKCCC investigators have used the MSMIMO SR, and more than 30 manuscripts are attributed to this SR. SKCCC Managed Shared Resource Reporting Period: January 1, 2020 to December 31, 2020

title: Impact of lymph node sparing on the anti-tumor response for head and neck cancer treated with radiation and immunotherapy
text:
The prognosis is poor for patients with advanced head and neck cancer (HNC) and scientists are investigating
whether radiotherapy and immunotherapy combinations can improve treatment outcomes; however, HNC
patients with high risks for regional metastasis typically receive RT targeted to their primary tumor site as well
as regional lymph nodes (RLN) in order to eradicate latent metastatic tumor cells. Using translational animal
models, including orthotopic murine head and neck cancer and spontaneous canine oral carcinoma, we will
define the impact of regional lymph node irradiation on the anti-tumor immune response for patients with head
and neck cancer treated with RT and immunotherapy (IO). If we demonstrate RT+IO and RLN sparing improves
outcomes in translational preclinical models of advanced HNC, the results of this project would challenge the
current standard of care and clinical paradigm surrounding radiation, immunotherapy, and elective RLN
irradiation for patients with advanced HNC.

title: Core A: Functional Genomics and Computational Integration Core
text:
To support the proposed functional genomic experiments and genomic analyses in Projects 1-3, this
Core will provide centralized technical and analytical leadership for harmonized gene inactivation studies and
support for the analysis, management, and sharing of genomics data. We will spearhead a Program-wide data
integration effort that will be critical to identify regulators of lineage plasticity in lung and prostate cancer, thus
advancing the goals of the Projects and enhancing their translational relevance.

title: Behavioral Genomics of Alcohol Neuroadaptation
text:
The Portland Alcohol Research Center (PARC) will perform in-depth multidisciplinary and integrative research
on mechanisms that impact risk for and consequences of heavy alcohol consumption, with a focus on the role
of a 4-part brain signaling complex known as the tetrapartite synapse (the pre-synaptic neuron, post-synaptic
neuron, glia, and extracellular matrix). In addition, the PARC will focus on the relationship of cognitive function
with alcohol drinking and the mechanisms under study. Findings will be integrated to provide comprehensive
information relevant to disease prediction and treatment.

title: Defining Vitamin C–Dependent Pathways in Extracellular Matrix Synthesis and Cell-Fate Transitions
text:
Abnormal extracellular matrix (ECM) accumulation is associated with a myriad of diseases, including pulmonary
fibrosis, cancer, and diabetes, yet the mechanisms by which cells meet the metabolic demands for ECM
synthesis remain poorly understood. The research proposed here will define how vitamin C-dependent metabolic
rewiring regulates ECM synthesis and, in turn, cell state transitions, providing insights into fundamental cellular
processes and identifying potential therapeutic targets for ECM-associated diseases.

title: Utility of Human Organoids for Safety and Efficiency Evaluations of Genome Editing Therapeutics
text: To enable safe and efficient advancement of genome editing therapeutics to the human clinical setting, it is essential to obtain preclinical data supporting safety and efficiency, but simple cell cultures and animal models have substantial limitations in predicting outcome in human tissues. Human organoids are 'mini-organ'-like structures grown in lab dishes that possess many key features of tissues, including diverse cell types in sophisticated arrangements specific to different organs, and disease phenotypes specific to individuals from whom they are derived. The objective of these studies is to blueprint a new predictive approach for genome editing efficiency and safety in human organoids, which can be used to de-risk strategies for regulatory consideration relevant to a wide variety of genome editing therapies.

title: Investigating the role of FGF21 in bone homeostasis in Duchenne Muscular Dystrophy
text:
Osteoporosis and fragility fractures affect 60% of patients with Duchenne Muscular Dystrophy (DMD) within
their second decade of life, yet there are no treatments to address this issue. This project will investigate the
role of fibroblast growth factor 21 (FGF21) in the pathogenesis of DMD-related osteoporosis. Our findings will
provide an improved understanding of the factors affecting osteoporosis in DMD and provide evidence for
future clinical trials targeting FGF21 to prevent bone loss in this patient population.

title: Cryo-EM structures of herpesvirus glycoprotein complexes in native membranes: insights into viral entry and immunity
text:
Varicella-zoster virus (VZV), the cause of chickenpox and shingles, can lead to serious complications like chronic
nerve pain and stroke. Our study will resolve the first high-resolution structures of essential VZV glycoproteins
using nanodiscs and cryogenic electron microscopy. These structures will uncover key mechanisms of
herpesvirus pathogenesis, immune evasion, and antibody binding and provide a structural framework for vaccine
optimization and antiviral development, potentially benefiting other herpesvirus-related conditions.

title: Molecular mechanisms of physical interactions between bacteria and their surroundings
text:
Type IV pili (T4P) are bacterial appendages that are critical for behaviors including DNA uptake during natural
transformation, biofilm formation, twitching motility, protein secretion, and virulence. Using several model
organisms with emphasis on Acinetobacter species, we will characterize the fundamental mechanisms driving
T4P dynamics, regulation, and function. This work will lay the groundwork for developing new methods to control
or hinder T4P and the broad behaviors they elicit in diverse bacterial pathogens.

title: HaMR Core
text:
The overarching goal of the Health and Metabolism Research (HaMR) Core is to graduate research project
leaders from COBRE support to R-series or equivalent independent funding. By doing so the HaMR core will
accelerate biomedical discovery, support a growing pool of competitive Alaskan investigators and foster Arctic-
inspired innovation for our most pressing health care challenges. By leveraging unique biological models, such
as hibernating mammals and sled dogs, the HaMR Core aims to inspire novel therapies for age-related
conditions, particularly frailty and dementia, which are increasingly relevant to Alaska’s aging population.
